1880: The person beside you laughed at their screen for two hours and never told you why. You'll wonder forever.
1881: At the belt you watched every bag that wasn't yours go by, twice, before yours appeared looking smug.
1882: Your neighbor's elbow eased over onto your side early and settled in like it owned the place. It did now.
1883: The person beside you asked where you were headed, and you smiled and said, honestly, it's complicated.
1884: Your seatmate guessed your whole life in three questions, got none of it right, and enjoyed it anyway.
1885: The sleeper beside you tilted slowly toward the window instead of you, and you felt oddly rejected.
1886: The passport line split into two, and you chose the one that would go slower, as you always somehow do.
1887: The seat in front eased back into your view, and you and your little screen became much closer friends.
1888: Your seatmate was very small and very serious and offered you exactly one cracker. You accepted, honored.
1889: The kid beside you counted everything on the plane out loud and reached a confident, wrong total.
1890: Your little seatmate showed you a drawing of the plane, and honestly it captured the mood exactly.
1891: You read the entire in-flight magazine, twice, and became an expert on subjects you'll never need again.
1892: Your seatmate wore enormous headphones and nodded to a beat only they could hear. You nodded too.
1893: The person beside you built a small fort of pillow and blanket and vanished into it without a word. Wise.
1894: Your neighbor read over your shoulder, gently and without shame, and seemed genuinely invested in your notes.
1895: You found your seat still warm and had to decide quickly how you felt about that. You moved on.
1896: Your seat had a button for everything and a working button for nothing. You sat upright and brave.
1897: The little one beside you waved at everyone who passed, running a tiny welcome committee from row nine.
1898: Your seatmate spread out with the calm certainty of a person who booked the whole row in their heart.
1899: The moment the plane stopped, the whole cabin stood at once and then waited, standing, for a long while.
1900: The cart rolled up, offered two choices, and you weighed them like the fate of nations hung on it.
1901: You got one small bag of pretzels and decided to make it last the whole flight. It did not last.
1902: The drink came in a cup so small you finished it in one polite sip and pretended that was plenty.
1903: They handed you the can and half a cup of ice and left you to pour it, a fully trusted professional.
1904: The tray came with a fork, a lid, and a small printed word naming a food you could not find on it.
1905: They asked if you wanted coffee, then poured before you answered, correctly guessing you would give in.
1906: The little bag held exactly seven peanuts. You know because you counted them, twice, out of respect.
1907: The snack cart squeaked up the aisle so slowly you had time to plan your whole order and then regret it.
1908: You opened the little bag carefully, and it opened all at once, gifting the row a light snowfall of crumbs.
1909: The tray came with a roll, a small square of butter, and the quiet challenge of combining them mid-air.
1910: You asked for just water, and it still arrived with a napkin, a straw, and a genuine sense of occasion.
1911: The dessert on the tray was the size of a coin and easily the most important part of the whole meal.
1912: Your fork arrived sealed in plastic with a napkin, a spoon, and a knife you would find no use for.
1913: The fizzy drink hissed open at altitude and foamed up over the cup, deeply excited to finally be here.
1914: Everything on the tray came in its own tiny sealed container, like a very small, very cautious meal.
1915: You chose the meal with no idea what it was, and it arrived confirming you still had no idea.
1916: The cart reached your row last, out of everything except the one thing you'd spent an hour deciding on.
1917: You held the little cup of coffee with both hands as the plane bumped, guarding it like treasure.
1918: The stir stick they gave you was shorter than the cup, which felt like a small joke at your expense.
1919: You saved half your snack for later, forgot about it, and found it flattened in a pocket days on.
